transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Petra 3 FP, Anselm 3 FP, Caddock 3 FP, Yarrow 3 FP. Face-up: The Hive Blight [H-02], Gullet Ford [L-01].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain hammers the reed banks as you come down off the causeway track to Gullet Ford, the only crossing south, water already waist-deep and climbing with a sound like a held breath. The sunken cart wreck out in the current marks where the last fools tried this without a guide. Somewhere behind the hiss of rain, faint and wrong, threads a thin ringing music — the swarm-song, carried on the wind from Saint Orrin's drowned belltower. Every one of you has a reason to be here and a reason to be afraid of the water. The ford is empty for now, but reeds tall as a man make good cover for anything that wants to watch you cross unseen.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The song's getting stronger—that's the swarm calling. The water's rising with it. We cross now, or we don't cross at all.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps into the shallows, reading the water's pull and the rising levels with practiced eyes, learned from years at the Ashwater Tollgate. She traces a path away from the sunken wreck, alert to movement in the reeds, then looks back to guide the others.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: That song carries the old liturgy beneath it—the bell-tongue is out there in the current, I'm certain. I'm going in.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (I stride toward the ford and wade into the churning water without hesitation, my ear straining hard against the rain to parse the swarm-song's layers. Beneath the insect-chorus, I catch the unmistakable cadences of ancient liturgy I've spent years studying—and beneath that, the resonance of drowned metal calling to me through the hive's own song. The bell-tongue is out there waiting. I lean forward into the current, following the pull.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: The ford's high and angry, but I know its moods. We cross east of that wreck where the current runs true and predictable. The reeds are thicker on the west—cover for things that shouldn't be trusted.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock steps to the ford's edge and reads the water with a midwife's practiced eye—the current's pull, the reed positions, the wreck's placement and how it breaks the flow. Her hands know how to find safe passage through any danger.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The current runs true down the middle. See how the water curves? That cart went wide into the deep channel. We go straight and strong, and we'll make the far side before the flood climbs further.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow crouches at the water's edge, reading the ford's currents with focused intensity. He releases Brack to scout the reed banks with a soft whistle while his eyes trace the water-flow like an old map, searching for the safe passage his family knew by heart.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: No, no—I can hear it, I can *hear* me in it—

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock — create advantage with Notice: dice + 0 + + → Superb (+5) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.text: Yarrow — create advantage with Notice: dice + 0 + + → Epic (+7) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Hold steady, boy. Tell me what moves in those reeds.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow accepts the compel on 'A Fisher's Stilt Hut'.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra stands rigid in the shallows, the swarm-song wrapping itself around her own name, and for a long moment she cannot move — until Yarrow's sharp whistle cuts through it and Brack barks at her heels, breaking the spell just enough. Caddock reads the water like a birth gone right, calling the safe line east of the wreck with total certainty, and Yarrow's eyes trace the true channel down the middle exactly as his family charts promised — between the two of them the crossing opens up clean and sure. Anselm wades in deeper than the others, ear cocked to the liturgy under the hive's drone, and for one held breath the current nearly takes him toward the drowned belltower's pull before he plants his feet and hauls himself back into the group's rhythm, the bell-tongue's call noted but not yet answered. Brack races the reed banks and comes back low and tense — something is out there, watching, but it doesn't strike. By the time the reeds close behind you, all four of you and the dog are standing dripping on the south bank, Gullet Ford crossed before the flood could close it.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I swore to guide them safely to the Order's temple sanctuaries across the drowned lands—to see them through to dry ground beyond the blight's reach. Yes, they still believe I owe that oath. Some of them trusted me with their lives when the reeds were shallower.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Those voices—I know those voices. I promised them sanctuary. I swore an oath.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm accepts the compel on 'A Pilgrim Band'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: A ragged column of Order pilgrims, bound to the Dry Saint's word and driven forward by their masters' command, come wading out of the rain at Gullet Ford. attacks at Gullet Ford using hooked spears thrust from the reed banks, because This is the same pilgrim band that once shared its scant bread with Anselm on the road — now the bread is gone, the rain hasn't stopped, and they've decided the party's dry stores belong to them instead..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The swarm-song fades just as another sound rises to replace it — voices raised in a ragged, familiar hymn, off-key and desperate. Out of the rain and reed banks they come wading, a column of pilgrims in sodden grey robes, hooked poles and fish-spears in their hands instead of prayer beads. Anselm knows their faces before he knows their intent: Old Maren, the twins from Hollowmoot, the boy who used to sing loudest. "Anselm!" one of them cries, half a plea and half an accusation, "you said you'd bring us to dry ground!" But their eyes are hollow, their steps too quick, and the hooked spears are already leveling at the party's packs — at the food, the dry gear, anything that isn't drowning. The safe line east of the wreck that Caddock called suddenly runs straight through them.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: They're hive-touched—the blight has them. This isn't bandits fighting hunger; the swarm is using them, pulling them toward us like fish on a line.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps into the shallows between her companions and the pilgrims, listening hard—not just with her ears, but with that deep part of her that hears the swarm-song winding through everything. The wrongness in them is unmistakable: the rigid jerking of limbs, the hollow set of their eyes, the way they move as one terrible chorus being pulled by invisible threads. She can almost feel the song's collar around their necks.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I see it in your eyes, Maren. The hive has you—you're not the ones who shared bread with me anymore. I'm sorry, but I won't die for ghosts.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm wades deeper into Gullet Ford toward Old Maren and the twins, his jaw set. He hears the swarm-song's echo in their hollow words, sees the wrongness in how they move too quick and empty. An exorcist knows hive-touch when he sees it. He draws his blade and drives toward their spear line, not to kill but to break through—to shatter their formation and force the crossing.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: You're starving, that's plain as water. But blood in this ford draws worse things than hunger ever could. We can share without dying.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock steps forward with the steady calm of someone who's guided people through every kind of crisis. She reads the column like she'd read a laboring woman at the breaking point—searching for the moment where choice still exists, where fury hasn't yet consumed the person underneath.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The water's talking. They've changed the line, but the line goes around. I can take us through.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow reads the water with practiced eyes, tracing how the current wraps around the pilgrim column—the eddies, the shallows where the ford has been redrawn. His hands move through the air as if charting unseen paths, pointing the way the water still runs safe and true.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The swarm's pull cannot fight four minds working as one. Petra's warning cuts clean through the panic — 'They're not choosing this!' — and something in her certainty steadies the whole crossing, so vivid that for a moment even the pilgrims seem to flinch at hearing their own wrongness named aloud. Anselm drives his blade-flat into the spear line, not to kill but to shatter it, and Old Maren staggers back clutching a numbed arm, the formation breaking apart into confused, jerking figures. Caddock's voice finds the cracks in the hive-song, calm and unhurried as a birth gone right, and for a breath two of the twins hesitate, spears lowering, something like recognition flickering behind hollow eyes — an opening. Yarrow reads the water around the chaos and calls the line true, threading the party and their dry stores around the wreck and through the gap Anselm tore open, Brack snapping at ankles that stray too close. They come out the far bank soaked, shaken, but whole — packs, food, and each other all still with them, the pilgrims' ragged hymn fading behind them into the rain.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I promised Coz safe passage out of the Sallowmere — real coin, merchant contacts, whatever it took to get him clear of the ferry life. When I was learning the Order's stolen bell-lore, he kept their people from asking questions, kept me hidden. I swore I'd get him out once I had the means. But the swarm-song pulled me deeper in, and I never came back to pay that debt.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I'll take you to the Temple, Coz. That's the first part of settling this. We'll work out the rest later.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts the compel on 'A Debt Called In'.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Kess, a Blackwater Cartel quartermaster I delivered a child for in fever-weather three winters back. Kess needs the Order's hoarded blight-cure lore—the Cartel's own people are showing hive-touch and they're desperate. The promised coin is what Kess can spare, but we both know it's borrowed against a future that might not come.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I see it in your eyes, Kess. The coin's smoke. But your people matter more than silver does—we go anyway.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock accepts the compel on 'Promise of Reward'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: Coz Marrow wades out of the reeds with two hard-eyed cousins at his back, calling in the debt he's owed — not in coin, but in a crossing. He says Petra knows exactly what she promised him, and he's brought witnesses so she can't pretend otherwise. begs the party to go to Coz wades closer, rain sluicing off his hood, and lays out the deal plain: he'll call the old debt square if Caddock and the rest guide him and his kin to Saint Orrin's Drowned Temple. 'I'm not asking you to work for free,' he says, and true to his word he offers coin for help — half now, pressed into Caddock's palm from a soaked purse, the rest when the job's done, if Caddock's old contact is to be believed., because her son followed the swarm-song into the belltower.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The rain doesn't let up as Coz falls into step beside Petra, his cousins fanning out behind with hooked poles held like they still don't trust this crossing — or her. Ahead, past drowned rooftops and a slack tangle of prayer-flags gone to rot, Saint Orrin's belltower rises grey and dry above the flood, the only clean line in a ruined skyline. The swarm-song is faint here, almost gentle, which everyone who's heard it before knows is the worst sign of all. Caddock's borrowed coin sits heavy and wrong in a pocket, half a promise from a quartermaster whose own people are dying by inches. Somewhere in that belltower is a boy who followed the sound past listening, and a debt, an oath, and a bargain all point the party toward the same drowned door.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: That gentle sound means he's already bound by it—the song calls gentle when it's already got them wrapped around the bones. We're going in after someone the hive has already marked, Coz, and we do this with eyes open.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra stops the group in their tracks, tilting her head to listen to the swarm-song's faint threads around the belltower. Her jaw tightens. She turns to face Coz and the others, her voice cut with certainty born from months of hearing this sound hunt for her own name.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I know these rites. I know where this song wants to take him. We go now, or the boy's already gone into the hive-dark, and no prayer pulls him back out.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm strides forward into the flood toward the belltower, his eyes locked on that grey stone rising above the drowning world. He recites fragments of Saint Orrin's old rites beneath his breath—not prayer, but anchor—using the liturgy he's read in ruined places to steady his mind against the swarm-song's pull. He's studied this Temple's layout in crumbling texts, knows the thresholds where the exorcism-wards should hold. He doesn't flinch from the faint, gentle call. That's when the hive hunts deepest.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: That song's different now—it's not hungry, it's satisfied. Like something's settled in the belltower and made itself a home. Your son didn't escape it, Coz; it pulled him in and kept him.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock halts at the threshold and raises her hand to pause the others. She closes her eyes and listens past the rain, past the water, to the faint swarm-song threading down from the belltower. She reads it the way she'd read any danger—with complete attention and the calm of someone who's delivered a hundred children in conditions that would break most people.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: There's a deeper channel running southeast of the tower—the water shows it plain if you know how to read. Brack's my bellwether; if he bristles, we stop, no arguments. That song's too quiet. Too gentle. That's when it's hunting.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow drops to one knee in the shallows, studying how the water moves around the belltower—the channels, the eddies, the places where the current runs clean. His fingers trace patterns in the flooded earth, reading the old ways like they're written into the mud itself. Brack paces the reed banks ahead, nose low, hackles faint, sensing something that goes deeper than ordinary marsh-danger. The tower shouldn't be this dry. Nothing that survives in this flood should stand that dry.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Anselm's murmured fragments of the old rites hold true — step by step through the shallows the swarm-song's faint, gentle pull slides off him like rain off oiled leather, and he reaches the threshold steady, eyes clear, the party following in the wake of his certainty. Caddock's focus goes deeper than the song itself: as she reads the water and the wards, her eye snags on something wrong at the tower's base — a scorched skiff wedged among the drowned pews, timbers still faintly char-black despite the endless rain, an oil flask bobbing empty in the flooded nave, and hoofprints pressed into the mud of the one dry sill, heading away toward the reeds. It's the same signature as the burned bridge Caddock's been turning over in her mind for weeks — someone came through here, and left in a hurry. Yarrow, meanwhile, has traced a deeper channel running southeast of the tower, clean water where the current doesn't fight the flood, a line Brack confirms with an easy, untroubled trot rather than his usual bristle. Between Anselm's anchor, Caddock's reading, and Yarrow's channel, the party reaches the temple's dry threshold together — Coz and his cousins close behind, the belltower's too-gentle song humming directly overhead now, and the drowned nave opening dark and waiting before them.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The water goes shallow and then vanishes entirely as you climb the last drowned stair into the nave, prayer-flags rotting overhead and the swarm-song humming faint through the stone like a held note. Lantern-light spills down from the belltower stair ahead — and with it, the shapes of grey-robed sentries, hooked poles crossed to bar the way, eyes going hard and wide the instant they mark Petra's face among you. Somewhere above, faint and patient, the bell-pattern Petra knows by heart keeps time with something that isn't wind. Coz and his cousins fall back into the shadows of the nave, unwilling to be seen this close to Order robes. The only dry ground for a mile, and it belongs to people who want Petra dead.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: That bell's ringing wrong, Brother Ilsan. You know it as well as I do. Let me through—I can fix this before the swarm reaches the bell chamber.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps forward deliberately, away from Coz and his cousins who've retreated into the shadows. She plants herself directly in front of Brother Ilsan, her hands open and visible. Her voice cuts clear and certain—the voice of someone who knows these bells better than the Order ever will.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I know the tongue of that bell, Brother. Your poles bar nothing from those who speak its language.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm strides forward through the rotting prayer-flags, his voice steady with the old words of exorcism, making clear through knowledge and certainty that he understands this bell—and what sings through it—far better than any sentry could. He is not asking permission to pass.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I'm Caddock, midwife of the Sallowmere. The water's still rising and we've nowhere else to go. We're not here to trouble your order—just to survive the night. Let us pass, or tell me what needs doing to buy passage.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock moves forward with the measured calm of someone who has delivered children in worse weather than this. She doesn't look at the spears; she looks at the men holding them—at the fear beneath the grey robes. She stops a respectful distance from the line and speaks as though addressing a frightened laboring mother: steady, certain, with the weight of someone who has walked through storms.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Hold, brothers. I'm Yarrow, Last of the Weir-Keepers. We're not here to bring the hive down on this place—we're running from it, same as you.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steps forward with the calm authority of a guard who's held many lines, Brack at his heel, reading Brother Ilsan's face and the sentries' stances with practiced precision. He marks the uncertainty in their grip, the hesitation in their eyes—these are duty-bound men, not true believers bent on slaughter.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Her hand stays steady. Brother Ilsan's robes fill her vision, and yeah, her gut twists with old anger—but she's got people standing behind her who didn't come this far to die in a temple nave. She keeps her fingers spread at her sides, open and empty.

transcript.text: Brother Ilsan's poles waver and drop as Anselm's exorcism-words land true — but old Sister Vell shoves through the sentry line, ledger-book clutched to her chest, and jabs a finger at Anselm: 'Every crossing owes. Your words bought passage, pilgrim — but the Order writes what's owed in blood-debt, not gratitude.' She scrawls Anselm's name into the ledger before he can stop her, binding him to a future claim the Order will collect however it likes.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Brother Ilsan's poles hit the flagstones with a wet clatter — whatever certainty held him rigid breaks against the weight of Petra's bell-lore and Anselm's true-spoken rite, and behind him the sentry line ripples, poles lowering one by one under Yarrow's steady, reasonable gaze. But Sister Vell is faster than any spear. She shoulders through the parting robes, ledger open, quill already moving, and stabs a bony finger at Anselm even as his words still hang in the damp air: "Every crossing owes, pilgrim. The Order does not forgive a debt just because the tongue that earned it was clever." Ink dries on his name before he can object — a blood-debt now written where the Order keeps its oldest, cruelest accounts, collectible however and whenever they choose. Still, the way is open. Ilsan steps aside, jaw tight, and the sentries part like reeds before a punt-pole, leaving the stair to the belltower clear ahead — the bell-pattern above ringing wrong, patient, and closer now than it was a moment ago.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The stair spirals up through cracked stone, the swarm-song growing from a hum to something almost like words the higher you climb. Sister Vell's threat of blood-debt still hangs in the air behind you, ledger unclosed, but ahead the belltower door stands ajar, grey light and rain-mist spilling through. Inside, the great bell hangs motionless and dry — and beneath it, something is singing that isn't the bell at all. Whatever answers here, in the one place the flood never reached, may be the truest shape of the hive yet.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The song has a rhythm... like the bell itself is trying to speak through it. It's not calling for me to freeze—it's calling for something else.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra climbs the final spiraling steps toward the belltower door, slowing her pace as the swarm-song rises from hum to almost-words. She closes her eyes and lets the bell-patterns she knows by heart wash over the stranger-singing, her ear trained from years at the Ashwater Tollgate where she learned to read every shift in water and weather. Her fingers find the stone rail and she traces it like a ledger, counting the rhythm beneath the chaos.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Show yourself. Answer me: are you the hive thinking, or just hunger wearing stolen words?

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm pushes toward the singing, murmuring fragments of Saint Orrin's old exorcism rites with each step up the spiraling stair. The words come automatic, muscle-memory of faith, but his mind is sharp and searching—he needs to know what sings beneath that bell. Is it the hive thinking? Or just hunger wearing stolen words?)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Hush now, whatever you are—I'm here. I know the hive-song, and I know what it does to folks. My name is Caddock, and my hands have never lost anyone in their need.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock pushes through the belltower door into the dry space beneath the hanging bell, her breathing steady and even. She moves toward the singing with the same focused calm she brings to any birth—reading the air, reading the source of the sound. Her hands are open at her sides, not defensive, and her eyes track where the singing pulls from.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Something's singing under there that shouldn't be singing. Hold position—let me see what it is before we move.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow climbs the final steps into the belltower, every muscle coiled. The swarm-song grows louder as he enters—not a hum anymore but something almost word-like, almost shaped. He moves toward the great bell, tilting his head to track the wrongness beneath it, searching the shadows and stone. His eyes—the same ones that read weir-gates and water-flow like maps of home—work the space methodically, looking for what isn't the bell at all.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The bell knows me. I'm listening alone.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's counting fingers find the pattern first — the swarm-song isn't one voice calling outward, it's echoing *inward*, looping back on itself like a bell struck from inside a jar. She reads the rhythm true: something small is caught in the note, not making it. Anselm's rite lands with total certainty and the words answer him back, wrong and right at once — not the hive thinking, not hunger wearing stolen words, but a voice too young to know it's singing at all. And Yarrow's eyes, trained on water and weir-gates, find her: tucked in a dry stone alcove behind the bell's swing-arc, knees to chest, throat raw, a girl no older than seven or eight, a weeping wound at her collarbone gone dark and threaded with something that pulses faint blue-grey under the skin in time with her humming. She doesn't stop singing when they find her. She doesn't seem to see them at all — eyes open, unfocused, fixed on nothing, the swarm-song pouring out of her like it's pouring *through* her from somewhere else entire. This is what called every hive-touched soul in the Sallowmere toward Saint Orrin's belltower: not a monster, not a priest gone holy-mad, but a lost child, hive-touched and used as a living bell-clapper for something further off and worse. The central question cracks open — and leaves a harder one in its place: what do you do with her now, with Sister Vell's blood-debt still unclosed on the stair behind you.

costs.tag: Freezes when the song calls her name
costs.text: As Petra opens her mouth to call the crossing order, the swarm-song shifts and threads her own name through its ringing — her feet root to the mudbank and the words die in her throat, just as the others need her call.

Through the rain and the tangle of the swarm-song, Yarrow spots it: his old fisher's stilt hut, still standing above the flood, its platform the only dry perch near the ford. Brack scrambles up onto it to get a better line on the reeds — but the rotten posts groan under his weight, ready to collapse
A ragged column of Order pilgrims, bound to the Dry Saint's word and driven forward by their masters' command, come wading out of the rain at Gullet Ford.

This is the same pilgrim band that once shared its scant bread with Anselm on the road — now the bread is gone, the rain hasn't stopped, and they've decided the party's dry stores belong to them instead.

The pilgrims sing their hymn loud and unhurried, Slow and Noisy enough that it carries clean over the rain and rolls right into the swarm-song's reach — hive-touched stir in the reeds as the ambush begins, and Anselm recognizes their voices before he sees their faces, freezing him with the weight of

Coz wades closer, rain sluicing off his hood, and lays out the deal plain: he'll call the old debt square if Caddock and the rest guide him and his kin to Saint Orrin's Drowned Temple. 'I'm not asking you to work for free,' he says, and true to his word he offers coin for help — half now, pressed in

Coz Marrow levels his hooked pole at her throat, cousins fanning out along the reed bank. 'Debts get paid in blood when they don't get paid in coin, Petra — you know that's how it's always been with us. Lead us to the Temple now, or it turns to violence right here at the ford, unpaid debts and all.'

Caddock's contact swears the coin is waiting at the Temple, but he won't meet Caddock's eyes when he says it — and something about that flinch says plain as words that the reward never materialises, that this promise is smoke, and the party's committing to the trip regardless.
